title: I drink tea every morning
goal: Use present-tense verbs for habits, make them negative with *ní*, and ask questions with *an*.
bekal: build the present tense of the first conjugation: *ólaim, ólann tú, ólaimid*
tell a habit (*Ólaim tae*) from something in progress (*Tá mé ag ól tae*)
use *ní* with séimhiú and *an* with urú

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Gnáthlá Bhudi
dialogs.intro: In class, Aoife asks each student to describe an ordinary day. It's Budi's turn.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: A Bhudi, inis dúinn faoi do lá. Cén t-am a éiríonn tú?
lines.id: Budi, tell us about your day. What time do you get up?
lines.literal: O Budi, tell to-us about your day. what time that rises you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Éirím ar a seacht. Ólaim tae agus ithim arán.
lines.id: I get up at seven. I drink tea and eat bread.
lines.literal: rise-I at the seven. drink-I tea and eat-I bread.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ní ólaim caife. Ní maith liom é.
lines.id: I don't drink coffee. I don't like it.
lines.literal: not drink-I coffee. not good with-me it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siúlaim chuig an scoil. Fanaim anseo go dtí a trí.
lines.id: I walk to school. I stay here until three.
lines.literal: walk-I to the school. stay-I here until the three.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: An dtuigeann tú gach rud sa rang?
lines.id: Do you understand everything in class?
lines.literal: question understands you every thing in-the class?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ní thuigim gach rud, ach tuigim go leor.
lines.id: I don't understand everything, but I understand plenty.
lines.literal: not understand-I every thing, but understand-I galore.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Maith thú! Cad a dhéanann tú tráthnóna?
lines.id: Well done! What do you do in the evening?
lines.literal: good you! what that does you evening?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Léim leabhar nó féachaim ar an teilifís. Uaireanta glanaim an chistin.
lines.id: I read a book or watch TV. Sometimes I clean the kitchen.
lines.literal: read-I book or look-I on the television. sometimes clean-I the kitchen.

notes: **Ólaim, but ólann tú.** Irish barely changes its verbs for different people. Only "I" and "we" have their own endings (*-aim* and *-aimid*); everyone else shares one form, *-ann*, plus the pronoun. So there are only **three** forms to learn per verb, not six.

**Ólaim tae isn't the same as Tá mé ag ól tae.** *Ólaim tae* means "I drink tea" — a habit, like the English present simple. *Tá mé ag ól tae* means "I'm drinking tea right now". English makes the same distinction, so you have a head start here. If the sentence has a word like *gach lá*, *go minic* or *uaireanta*, it almost certainly takes the habitual form.

**Ní thuigim, an dtuigeann tú — two small words that change letters.** *Ní* ("not") brings **séimhiú**: *tuigim* → *ní thuigim*, *canaim* → *ní chanaim*. *An* (question) brings **urú**: *tuigeann* → *an dtuigeann*, *canann* → *an gcanann*. Words starting with a vowel are untouched by both: *ólaim* → *ní ólaim*, *an ólann tú?*

**The verb comes first.** *Ólaim tae* — verb, then object. If the doer is named, it goes in the middle: *Ólann Seán tae* ("Seán drinks tea"). This verb–subject–object order is the same in every tense, so once you're used to it, it won't trouble you again.

blocks.text: The first conjugation is verbs whose base form has one syllable: *ól, fan, can, glan, dún, léigh, tuig, cuir*. Their endings depend on the last vowel of the base — **broad** (a, o, u) or **slender** (e, i).

Say them like this: *ólaim* = OH-lim, *ólann* = OH-lan, *ólaimid* = OH-lih-mid, *tuigim* = TIH-gyim, *tuigeann* = TIH-gyan. The endings *-ann* and *-eann* both sound like a short "an"; the *e* is only there to show that the consonant before it is slender.

blocks.title: Two forms that break the pattern
items: *Léim* means "I read" — but it also happens to mean "a jump" as a noun. Only its place in the sentence tells them apart.
The "we" form can also be written as two words: *ólann muid* is just as correct as *ólaimid*, and more often heard in Connacht and Ulster.

sections.title: Habits — and the words that signal them

blocks.title: Compare for yourself
items: *Ólaim tae.* — I drink tea. A habit, not tied to any moment.
*Tá mé ag ól tae.* — I'm drinking tea. Right now, in front of you.

*Ólaim tae gach maidin, ach tá mé ag ól caife anois.* — "I usually drink tea every morning, but right now I'm drinking coffee." This sentence has both at once, and it's worth memorizing as a reference point.

exercises.prompt: Write the "I" form of these verbs.
Make these negative. Remember *ní* brings séimhiú.
Turn these into questions. Remember *an* brings urú.
Choose the habitual form or the *ag* form, then translate.

answers: ólaim — fanaim — glanaim — tuigim — cuirim — léim
Ní ólaim caife. — Ní thuigim an cheist. — Ní chanaim gach lá. — Ní ghlanann sé an chistin. — Ní fhanann siad sa bhaile. — Ní itheann tú feoil.
An ólann tú tae? — An dtuigeann tú Gaeilge? — An gcanann sí go minic? — An bhfanann sibh anseo? — An nglanann siad an teach? — An itheann sé arán?
Ólaim tae gach maidin. — Tá mé ag ól tae anois. — Siúlann sí chuig an scoil go minic. — Tá sí ag siúl chuig an scoil. — Ní ólaim caife riamh. — Tá muid ag glanadh na cistine.
